web_title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Balance Sheet
book_title: Chapter 6: Following the Cash — 10-Year Financials & Earnings Quality
title: Following the Cash
question: How much of Xpro's reported profit is real, recurring cash earnings, and can the balance sheet carry a ₹700 Cr expansion until the new lines earn their cost?

epigraph.quote: unrealised non-cash adjustments to Euro denominated borrowings, repayable over 10 years
epigraph.author: Xpro India Q1 FY26 investor release, 28 Jul 2025, explaining the June-quarter profit fall [90]

web_blocks.html: This chapter uses the audited FY26 annual report (Walker Chandiok, unmodified opinion), earlier reports, company decks and the Screener roll-up. Quarterly and H1 FY27 figures are unaudited. Where Screener and the company differ we use the company figure. Consolidated, ₹ Cr, years to 31 March unless stated [8][17].

web_blocks.caption: Ten-year profit and loss (Screener consolidated, ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Sales roughly doubled from ₹259 Cr (FY15) to ₹505 Cr (FY26; TTM ₹592 Cr). Operating margin fell from 15% (FY23) to 6% (company EBITDA before FX: 9.4%). Net profit fell from ₹45 Cr to ₹20 Cr (TTM ₹35 Cr).

web_blocks.caption: Ten-year balance sheet (Screener consolidated, ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Reserves jumped from ₹215 Cr to ₹538 Cr in FY24 on the QIP and warrants. Borrowings (with leases) rose from ₹39 Cr to ₹325 Cr. Screener's Sep-26 split of fixed assets ₹712 Cr and CWIP ₹44 Cr is misclassified. The company shows PPE ₹351 Cr, leased land ₹44 Cr and CWIP ₹360 Cr [14].

web_blocks.caption: Ten-year cash flow (Screener consolidated, ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Operating cash flow fell from ₹83 Cr (FY23) to ₹13 Cr and ₹20 Cr in FY25-FY26, while free cash flow fell from +₹47 Cr to -₹274 Cr and -₹120 Cr. Financing inflows of ₹278 Cr, ₹203 Cr and ₹151 Cr funded the build.

web_blocks.caption: Ten-year working-capital and return ratios (Screener consolidated)
web_blocks.takeaway: ROCE fell from 25% (FY23) to 4% (FY26) as capital outgrew profit. The cash conversion cycle stretched from 33 to 80 days. Inventory days were 76 and payable days fell from 68 to 46.

web_blocks.title: Revenue, margin and profit: the bridge

web_blocks.html: Between FY23 and FY26 revenue was flat (₹511.0 Cr to ₹505.5 Cr). EBITDA before FX fell from ₹74.4 Cr to ₹47.4 Cr, a margin drop of 5.2 points (14.6% to 9.4%). Our calculation splits the drop into three parts. Gross margin accounts for 0.9 points (31.5% to 30.6%). Employee cost accounts for 1.5 points (₹30.1 Cr to ₹37.6 Cr). Other expenses account for 2.7 points (₹56.4 Cr to ₹69.5 Cr), largely build-up ahead of the new lines [39][36].

web_blocks.caption: Screener operating profit versus company EBITDA (₹ Cr)
rows: Company EBITDA before FX / Screener OP
web_blocks.takeaway: The two bases tie until FY26, when Screener's operating profit is ₹15.4 Cr lower because it leaves the FX loss in expenses [36][8].

web_blocks.html: The FY26 gap and the June-2025 quarter. The ₹15.4 Cr gap is the consolidated unrealised FX loss of ₹15.84 Cr. Of this, ₹11.14 Cr sits at the parent on the Bpifrance euro loan, and about ₹5 Cr or AED 1.95 mn sits in the UAE subsidiary. The company shows the loss below EBITDA [8][101]. The same mechanism explains Screener's -₹2.52 Cr operating profit for June 2025. Company EBITDA was +₹14.3 Cr on revenue of ₹144.9 Cr. The quarter's consolidated unrealised FX loss was about ₹16.8 Cr (H1 ₹19.9 Cr less Q2 ₹3.1 Cr), and ₹14.3 Cr less ₹16.8 Cr is -₹2.5 Cr. It was not an operating loss. Production was 9,165 t, up 7.7% y/y [90].

web_blocks.caption: Quarterly trend, Sep 2023 to Sep 2026 (Screener consolidated; unaudited; ₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: Sales swing with refrigerator seasonality and polymer prices. OPM has slid from 15.8% to an 8-12% band on price cuts, cost build-up and FX noise [17].

web_blocks.html: H1 FY27 (unaudited). Revenue was ₹351.1 Cr (+32.6%), EBITDA ₹31.0 Cr (8.8%) and PAT ₹14.8 Cr against -₹0.5 Cr in H1 FY26. The new line's costs are now in the P&L. Q2 depreciation was ₹5.2 Cr against ₹3.0 Cr, and finance cost was ₹3.2 Cr against ₹1.7 Cr. As a result, PBT of ₹10.5 Cr on 47% higher sales is only 56% above last year's ₹6.7 Cr [36][97].

web_blocks.caption: Where profit came from (consolidated, ₹ Cr)
rows: PBT before other income, FX and exceptional items (our calculation)
web_blocks.takeaway: Excluding treasury income and FX, pre-tax profit has halved from ₹55.3 Cr to ₹27.9 Cr. Also, 60% of FY26 reported PBT was other income [8][36].

web_blocks.html: Treasury income is mostly interest on equity cash and shrinks as cash is spent. Standalone deposit interest fell from ₹16.16 Cr to ₹11.33 Cr. Standalone FY26 other income also holds a ₹3.65 Cr intragroup guarantee fee and a ₹2.29 Cr one-off insurance claim [8]. FX: about 95% of gross debt is euro-linked. Against it stand ₹46.5 Cr of derivatives on about ₹274 Cr of exposure, roughly 17% covered (our calculation). A 1% EUR/INR move is about ₹2.7 Cr, or 9% of FY26 PBT. A 10% move is about ₹27 Cr, near a year's PBT. Tax: standalone ETR was 26.1% against 35.6% consolidated because subsidiary losses are not tax-effected. The subsidiary reports it qualifies for 0% free-zone tax, so we expect the gap to narrow as it earns (our inference) [101]. Prior items: FY24 carried a ₹2.02 Cr "right to recompense" bank charge. FY22 had a ₹4.55 Cr deferred-tax credit against a ₹14.11 Cr charge in FY23 [37].

Capitalised interest. Barjora-2's ₹212.34 Cr moved to PPE on 27 March 2026 "including borrowing costs". This is a key audit matter the auditor accepted, and the interest amount is undisclosed [8]. Our triangulation starts from about ₹263 Cr of average debt at 3.5-3.8%. That implies ₹9.2-10.0 Cr of gross interest against ₹4.36 Cr expensed. Roughly ₹5 Cr (16-19% of FY26 PBT) was therefore capitalised. That interest now hits the P&L, which with ₹2.2 Cr more quarterly depreciation doubled H1 FY27 finance cost. The UAE line's interest stays capitalised until start-up [36].

web_blocks.caption: Cash conversion (₹ Cr)
web_blocks.takeaway: CFO converted 67% of EBITDA across FY23-FY26 but 47% across FY24-FY26. The gap is working capital, with ₹78 Cr absorbed from FY24 to H1 FY27 [36][17].

web_blocks.html: Interest income sits in investing, so CFO excludes the ₹13.7 Cr received in FY26 and is conservative against profit. Screener's CFO/EBITDA row (110%, 80%, 54%, 99%) divides pre-tax CFO by its own operating profit. FY26's 99% is ₹31.4 Cr over ₹32 Cr, whereas after-tax CFO over company EBITDA is 43% (our calculation) [17][8]. Why working capital grew. Inventory days rose from 49 to 76 because management holds "at least 3 months of stock" of an imported specialty resin. Standalone raw-material stock rose from ₹36.74 Cr to ₹49.76 Cr, while finished goods stayed near ₹17-18 Cr [89][8]. Payable days fell from 68 to 46 as Q4 purchases fell with sales. Capex creditors also shrank from ₹12.4 Cr to ₹2.2 Cr. In H1 FY27 receivables rose ₹24 Cr to ₹93.2 Cr [36]. This is policy, not manipulation, but it consumes cash.

Screener's Sep-2026 fixed assets of ₹712 Cr and CWIP of ₹44 Cr appear swapped. The ₹712 Cr equals PPE ₹351.3 Cr plus CWIP ₹360.0 Cr plus intangibles ₹0.9 Cr. The ₹44 Cr equals right-of-use assets of ₹44.3 Cr (our reconciliation). On the company's figures PPE, leased land and CWIP total about ₹756 Cr, 61% of ₹1,241 Cr of assets. The ₹360 Cr of CWIP is the UAE line earning nothing yet [14][36].

web_blocks.caption: Debt schedule (₹ Cr)
rows: EURIBOR + 1.21%; instalments from Apr 2027 per subsidiary accounts
Hermes cover; parent guarantee EUR 23.72 mn (₹256.4 Cr); machinery pledged
web_blocks.takeaway: The loans are export-credit backed and low-coupon, but nearly all euro-linked. They fund assets that will earn rupees, dirhams and dollars [8][101][102].

web_blocks.html: Standalone versus consolidated. On the 4 November call management said "Total borrowings stood at INR106.7 crores". Consolidated borrowings are ₹273.7 Cr because the AKA loan (about ₹154 Cr) sits in the subsidiary [52]. Cash and bank balances were ₹300.4 Cr in March 2026 (parent ₹175.3 Cr, subsidiary about ₹125 Cr). They were ₹233.4 Cr in September, of which ₹64.3 Cr is raised money pending use. The group moved from net cash of ₹11.6 Cr to net debt of ₹40.3 Cr (₹82.6 Cr with leases; our calculation). Debt/equity is 0.34, and audited standalone DSCR was 2.24 against 3.28 [2]. Interest cover on EBITDA less depreciation fell from 8.4x (FY23) to 4.7x (FY26) and 3.2x in H1 FY27 (our calculation).

Repayment burden. The subsidiary's audited accounts show the AKA loan wholly non-current with instalments from April 2027, which the arithmetic supports. Consolidated current borrowings of ₹44.55 Cr equal the parent's ₹18.41 Cr plus the subsidiary's ₹26.1 Cr overdraft [101][2]. On drawn amounts the burden is about ₹14 Cr of principal in FY27, then from FY28 about ₹29 Cr of principal plus ₹10 Cr of interest. That is roughly ₹39 Cr a year (our calculation), against FY26 CFO of ₹20.4 Cr. A 13 November 2026 postal ballot proposes refinancing into Emirates Development Bank facilities (parent guarantee up to AED 83 mn). It also proposes up to ₹60 Cr of loans and ₹60 Cr of equity or loans to the subsidiary [103].

web_blocks.caption: Returns versus an assumed 12% cost of capital
rows: ROIC, NOPAT at 25.17% on PBT plus interest (our calculation)
web_blocks.takeaway: Equity grew 3.4x (₹233.6 Cr to ₹798.4 Cr) while EBITDA fell 36%. Excluding ₹299.5 Cr of UAE CWIP, FY26 ROIC would be 5.4%, still below the hurdle [104][36].

web_blocks.html: The 12% is our assumption, not a company or market figure. It is about 14% on the 72% equity share of capital plus about 4.5% on euro debt, rounded up. At 10% the FY26 spread is still -6.6 points. Company RoCE differs by deck (5.3% in May, 5.7% in November). The post-tax hurdle below adds ₹34 Cr of depreciation (₹680 Cr over 20 years) and uses gross cost.

web_blocks.caption: Utilisation of the 9,000 t programme needed to earn its cost (capex ₹680 Cr, ₹7.6 lakh per tonne; our calculation)
web_blocks.takeaway: A 12% post-tax return on gross cost needs near-full utilisation at a 40% margin. Only the top of management's 35-55% range makes it comfortable.

web_blocks.caption: Per-share record (units: crore shares; Screener EPS is bonus-adjusted)
rows: Dividend per share (₹) / cash payout on PAT
web_blocks.takeaway: The count nearly doubled, and half of the increase was a 1:2 bonus. Ex-bonus dilution was 32.4%. EPS fell 68% against a 56% fall in profit [17][8].

web_blocks.html: Units check: the share count is 1.18 crore (1,18,13,500) in March 2022 and 2.35 crore (2,34,70,391) in March 2026. The ₹11.8 Cr and ₹23.5 Cr are share capital at ₹10 face value [2]. Warrants at ₹762 and ₹975 and the QIP at ₹1,101 supplied the non-bonus shares at their contractual issue prices [31][105]. Book value per share rose from about ₹97 (bonus-adjusted FY22) to ₹324, or 3.3x. EPS over closing book value therefore fell from about 26% to 2.5% (our calculation; the company's FY26 RoE is 4.6% on average equity) [104]. Dividends stayed at ₹2 a share, ₹20.2 Cr in total, which is 4.6% of the ₹440 Cr raised. Promoters fell from about 50% to 40.31% while their absolute shares rose slightly [92].

web_blocks.title: Sources and uses of cash, FY22-FY26

web_blocks.caption: Cumulative sources and uses (₹ Cr; Screener cash flow totals plus audited raises; our calculation)
web_blocks.takeaway: Equity of about ₹520 Cr roughly equals cumulative capex of ₹507 Cr, so shareholders funded the build. Operating cash flow and net other financing ended up largely in deposits and cash.

web_blocks.html: FY22-FY24 capex was about ₹80 Cr against CFO of ₹176 Cr. FY25-FY26 consolidated capex was ₹428 Cr (parent ₹143 Cr, subsidiary ₹285 Cr) against CFO of ₹33 Cr, 13 times. In FY26 alone the parent's CFO of ₹24.2 Cr matched its capex of ₹24.3 Cr. The burn sat in the subsidiary. In May 2024 management said "Our cash generation looks strong enough to have supported it without these raises". The record shows ₹77 Cr of CFO over FY24-FY26 against about ₹465 Cr of capex [38]. ₹300 Cr of cash in March 2026 is 68% of the parent equity raised. Management's per-plant revenue guide is ₹150-200 Cr [39].

web_blocks.caption: Accounting and balance-sheet scorecard
rows: Unmodified; KAMs on CWIP capitalisation and revenue [8]
Dividends only; nil pledge [33]; contingent liabilities about ₹5.2 Cr, 0.7% of net worth [8]
Undisclosed; our estimate about ₹5 Cr in FY26 [8]
CFO 25% and 43% of EBITDA; CCC 33 to 80 days [17]
Debt 8x; net debt ₹40 Cr; guarantee ₹256 Cr [36][102]
Q4 deck showed Mar-25 ROU ₹344.5 Cr and CWIP ₹37.0 Cr, transposed; RoCE varies by deck; ₹106.7 Cr vs ₹273.7 Cr debt [52][36]
About 17% covered; 1% EUR/INR = ₹2.7 Cr; FY26 loss ₹15.8 Cr [8]
web_blocks.takeaway: Nothing in the accounting is red. The single red flag is an economic exposure, not a reporting one.

web_blocks.html: Earnings quality: our verdict. Accounting quality is high. Audits are clean, tax is paid and there is no related-party leakage. The FX loss behind the June-2025 "operating loss" is non-cash and disclosed. Economic quality is weaker than reported profit. About 60% of FY26 PBT was other income, and underlying pre-tax profit fell from ₹55 Cr to ₹28 Cr. Deliberate stocking also holds back cash. FY26 is better read as about ₹28 Cr of operating profit plus a shrinking treasury cushion.

Balance-sheet risk: our verdict. The balance sheet is not stressed today. Net debt is ₹40 Cr on ₹813 Cr of equity, cash is ₹233 Cr and the debt is export-credit backed at low coupons. The risk is structural and sits in the next 18 months. It comes from euro debt whose 10% swing is about a year's PBT and a ₹256 Cr parent guarantee. It also comes from about ₹39 Cr a year of debt service from FY28 and a ₹358 Cr asset earning nothing until the UAE line starts. The balance sheet can absorb a delay of a few quarters, not a prolonged one without refinancing.

book_paragraphs: Now we get to follow the money, and I want you to see it the way an auditor would: not as a story, but as a trail. Xpro's ten-year numbers have a clear shape. Sales roughly doubled, from ₹259 crore in FY15 to ₹505 crore in FY26. Profit climbed to about ₹45 crore a year in FY22 and FY23 and has since fallen to ₹20 crore. Meanwhile the balance sheet more than tripled, from ₹340 crore of assets in FY23 to ₹1,218 crore in FY26. Revenue flat, profit down, assets up three and a half times. How did that happen, and is it the kind of thing that ends well?

Start with the margin. Between FY23 and FY26 revenue barely moved, ₹511 crore to ₹505 crore, but EBITDA, which is operating profit before depreciation and interest, fell from ₹74 crore to ₹47 crore. The margin dropped five points, from 14.6 percent to 9.4 percent. About a point is thinner gross margin. About a point and a half is higher employee cost. Nearly three points is other expenses, up 23 percent while sales did not move. Much of that is staff and overhead built ahead of the new lines, in management's words "higher expenses necessary for the buildup ahead of expansion" (30 May 2025) [39]. The plant that will earn the money is already on the payroll; the money has not arrived.

Then there is the quarter that frightened people. On Screener, the data site that summarises Indian company financials, the June 2025 quarter shows an operating loss of ₹2.5 crore. It looks like a disaster. It was not. The company's own EBITDA that quarter was a positive ₹14.3 crore. The difference is almost exactly the euro loan. Xpro borrowed about 25 million euros to pay for its machines, and when the euro strengthened against the rupee, the accounting rules forced it to mark up what it owed, a loss of about ₹16.8 crore that quarter, none of it cash. The company said so at the time, pointing to "unrealised non-cash adjustments to Euro denominated borrowings, repayable over 10 years" [90]. That is a fair explanation. But notice the other half of the lesson. Only about a sixth of the exposure was covered by derivatives, so a 1 percent move in the euro is about ₹2.7 crore, and a 10 percent move is about ₹27 crore, close to a whole year's profit before tax. Warren Buffett's line applies: "Only when the tide goes out do you discover who's been swimming naked."

Now read the quarters themselves, with a warning that they are unaudited. From September 2023 to September 2026, sales bounced between ₹96 crore and ₹177 crore a quarter, following refrigerator seasons and plastic-resin prices. The operating margin slid from 15.8 percent in December 2023 to between 8 and 12 percent, apart from the June 2025 distortion. In the half to September 2026 sales were ₹351 crore, up 32.6 percent, EBITDA ₹31 crore and profit ₹14.8 crore against a small loss a year earlier. But the new Barjora line's costs are now in the accounts: in the September quarter depreciation was ₹5.2 crore against ₹3.0 crore and finance cost ₹3.2 crore against ₹1.7 crore. So profit before tax of ₹10.5 crore on sales that were 47 percent higher was only 56 percent above last year's ₹6.7 crore.

Next, what the profit is made of. Of FY26's ₹30 crore pre-tax profit, ₹18 crore, 60 percent, was other income, and 82 percent of that was interest on the cash raised from shareholders. That income shrinks as the cash is spent. Take out other income and the FX loss and underlying pre-tax profit falls from ₹55 crore in FY23 to ₹28 crore in FY26. I would not call that a flaw in the accounts. I would call it the honest size of the business that is already running, with a treasury cushion under it that is being used up. Two more details. The tax rate looks odd, 35.6 percent consolidated against 26.1 percent at the parent, because the losses of the UAE subsidiary earn no tax credit; the subsidiary says it qualifies for the zero-percent free-zone rate, so I expect the gap to narrow once it earns (my inference) [101]. And interest on money borrowed to build an asset is, by the rules, added to the asset's cost until it starts working. The company does not say how much, but by my triangulation about ₹5 crore was capitalised in FY26, 16 to 19 percent of pre-tax profit. The auditors treated it as a key audit matter and accepted it. From late March 2026 that interest is expensed on Barjora, which is one reason finance cost doubled this half.

Then the cash. A profit is an opinion, as accountants say; cash is a fact. In FY23 the business generated ₹83 crore of cash from operations, 111 percent of EBITDA. By FY25 that was ₹13 crore, 25 percent, and FY26 was ₹20 crore, 43 percent. The reason is working capital, the money tied up in stock and unpaid bills. Inventory days went from 49 to 76, because management holds "at least 3 months of stock in the plant" of a specialty plastic resin that must be imported and is vulnerable to shipping disruption. Supplier days fell from 68 to 46. The cash conversion cycle, the days between paying for materials and collecting from customers, went from 33 to 80. Over FY24 to the first half of this year about ₹78 crore was absorbed. A careful reader would also note that Screener shows a much kinder 99 percent cash conversion for FY26. That divides pre-tax cash flow by an operating profit that already carries the FX loss; after tax, over the company's EBITDA, the number is 43 percent. I read the stocking as policy, a prudent response to a conflict near the Gulf, not manipulation, but it costs cash all the same.

Now the balance sheet. A housekeeping point first. Screener's September 2026 column shows fixed assets of ₹712 crore and construction in progress of ₹44 crore. These appear swapped. The company's own statement shows plant of ₹351 crore, leased land of ₹44 crore and construction in progress, CWIP for short, of ₹360 crore. The ₹712 crore is plant plus CWIP and the ₹44 crore is the lease. CWIP is the UAE plant, still being built and earning nothing. I use the company's numbers throughout.

On debt, the picture changed from almost nothing to meaningful. Gross borrowings were ₹36 crore in March 2023 and ₹289 crore in March 2026, eight times as much. They are almost all euro loans backed by European export-credit agencies, at 3.84 percent fixed or the euro interbank rate plus 1.21 percent. Cash and bank balances were ₹300 crore in March and ₹233 crore in September, so the group went from net cash of ₹12 crore to net debt of ₹40 crore. Interest cover, the number of times operating profit covers interest, fell from 8.4 to 3.2 times. On the 4 November call management said "Total borrowings stood at INR106.7 crores." That is the parent only. The consolidated figure is ₹273.7 crore, because the UAE subsidiary carries about ₹154 crore of its own, which the parent guarantees up to ₹256 crore. About ₹125 crore of the group's March cash sat in that subsidiary.

When does the bill arrive? The subsidiary's own audited accounts, which I read, show that its loan begins repaying in April 2027, and consolidated current borrowings add up only if that is true. So the burden is gentler this year and heavier from FY28: roughly ₹39 crore a year of principal and interest on today's drawn amounts, against an operating cash flow of ₹20 crore last year. Until the new lines earn, the cash is the bridge. And on 13 November 2026 the company sent shareholders a postal ballot to refinance the subsidiary's debt into facilities from the Emirates Development Bank, with a parent guarantee up to 83 million dirhams and room for another ₹60 crore of loans and ₹60 crore of equity or loans. A skeptic reads that as a sign the funding is not finished. A bull reads it as ordinary treasury management by a company that kept its rating at A-.

Does the new capital earn its keep? I use a hurdle I want to be explicit about: a 12 percent cost of capital, which is my assumption, not the company's. Return on invested capital, ROIC, which is the after-tax operating profit on the capital working in the business, was about 21 percent in FY23 and 3.4 percent in FY26. Against 12 percent that is a surplus of ₹21 crore in FY23 and a shortfall of ₹70 crore in FY26. The equity base grew 3.4 times while EBITDA fell by a third. To earn a 12 percent EBITDA return on the ₹680 crore for the two new lines, about 70 percent use at a 30 percent margin and ₹430 a kilo is needed. To earn a 12 percent after-tax return, near-full use at a 40 percent margin. Those are the stakes.

A quick check on shares, because people stumble here. The share count is 1.18 crore in 2022 and 2.35 crore in 2026, not 11.8 and 23.5; those are the share capital in rupee crore. Half the increase was a free bonus, so the true dilution is about 32 percent. Yet earnings per share fell 68 percent while profit fell 56 percent. Book value per share went from about ₹97 to ₹324. The dividend stayed at ₹2 a share for five years, ₹20 crore in total, 4.6 percent of the ₹440 crore raised. Charlie Munger said, "Show me the incentives and I'll show you the outcome." Here the money went into factories, not into payouts.

Now the full trail, FY22 to FY26. The business generated ₹209 crore of operating cash. Shareholders added ₹440 crore at the parent and ₹80 crore at the UAE subsidiary. That funded ₹507 crore of capex, and what remained went into deposits and cash. In May 2024 Bhaskar said "Our cash generation looks strong enough to have supported it without these raises." The record is ₹77 crore of cash generation over three years against about ₹465 crore of capex. The raises were not optional, and they arrived early: ₹300 crore of cash, 68 percent of what the parent raised, was still on the balance sheet in March 2026.

Let me walk you through the scorecard the way I would an examiner's checklist. Two lines are green: the unmodified audit opinion, and the related-party dealings, pledges and contingent liabilities, which come to dividends only, nothing, and about ₹5 crore, under 1 percent of net worth [8]. Six lines are amber, meaning worth watching rather than worrying: the undisclosed capitalised interest, the dependence on other income, the cash conversion, the leverage and guarantees, the dilution, and the consistency of disclosure. On that last one, the company's own fourth-quarter deck swapped two lines for March 2025, showing leased land as ₹344.5 crore and construction in progress as ₹37.0 crore when the audited figures are the reverse; return on capital for FY26 appears as 5.3 percent in one document and 5.7 percent in another. These are presentation errors, not accounting ones, but a careful reader likes consistency [36]. One is red: the unhedged euro exposure.

How would a bull and a skeptic each read the cash burn? The bull says free cash flow of minus ₹274 crore and minus ₹120 crore is the price of building two lines that management says will each add ₹150 to ₹200 crore of revenue [39], that the parent itself was roughly self-funding in FY26 and the burn sat in the subsidiary, and that the debt is low-coupon and long-dated. The skeptic answers that operating cash flow was only ₹33 crore across the two years, that capex ran at 13 times it, that the UAE plant is well over a year behind its first guidance, and that every quarter of delay adds interest and depreciation without revenue. Both are describing the same numbers. The difference is the date the UAE plant starts and how quickly the new Barjora line fills.

So what is my verdict? On accounting quality I give a green. The audit is clean, tax is paid, related-party flows are small and nothing is pledged. On economic earnings quality I would say it is weaker than the headline: the operating base is about ₹28 crore before other income and FX, not ₹30 crore plus. On the balance sheet, the risk is not that it is weak today, because it is not. It is that it rests on euro debt that is largely uncovered, a parent guarantee and a ₹358 crore plant that has to start. The one red flag in my scorecard is that exposure, and it is a risk of volatility, not of dishonesty. A balance sheet can absorb a few quarters of delay. It cannot absorb many.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: The tidy way to read this chapter is that the accounts are honest and the business is in transition. Honest accounts mean you can trust the trail: raise equity early, spend it on factories, let the margin sag while costs arrive before volume. What the trail cannot tell you is whether the new lines will earn their cost. For that you need the numbers this chapter keeps pointing to: utilisation, realisation and the date the UAE plant starts. Until they arrive, a margin of safety lives in the cash on the balance sheet and in the export-credit terms of the debt, and both have limits.
